name: Environmentalism
summary: Environmentalism seeks to protect and restore natural systems and to make human use of them sustainable. Its adherents back regulation, urgent climate action and the value of nature beyond its use to people, and are divided on technology, nuclear power, economic growth and ownership. Beyond ecology it has little doctrine, so many social and economic questions are left to its strands.
scope: The mainstream modern environmental movement and its political expression in green politics, drawing on Leopold's land ethic, the Brundtland report, Carson-era conservation and the SEP's account of environmental ethics. It excludes free-market environmentalism and eco-fascism as minority or fringe strands, and answers dark-green and bright-green splits as 0 or low where adherents divide.

keyFigures.name: Aldo Leopold
keyFigures.role: Author of the land ethic, a founding text of ecological ethics.

keyFigures.name: John Muir
keyFigures.role: Preservationist and Sierra Club co-founder who held nature has inherent rights.

keyFigures.name: Rachel Carson
keyFigures.role: Author of Silent Spring, which spurred modern environmental awareness.

sources.title: Green politics
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Four pillars, nuclear, growth, decentralization, economic strands.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Environmentalism has no healthcare doctrine; the green-politics strand pairs ecological wisdom with social justice, and environmental justice stresses pollution-linked health burdens, so mild support is inferred.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not an environmental issue; inferred from the social-justice pillar of green politics and labor environmentalism's alliance with unions.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Environmentalists hold that markets ignore ecological damage and non-priced species, as Leopold argued of economic motives; free-market environmentalism is a minority strand.

public-ownership.rationale: Green strands split between eco-socialists who favour public or cooperative ownership and eco-capitalists and green liberals who accept regulated markets.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Not central to the ideology; the Brundtland report stresses poverty and equity, and greens favour a tax shift mainly onto pollution rather than wealth, so support is weak.

unions-good.rationale: Labor environmentalism seeks union alliances and a just transition, but unions are not a core environmental tenet.

property-fundamental.rationale: Leopold argued land ownership carries obligations beyond self-interest, and environmentalism accepts overriding property rights through regulation to protect ecosystems.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Mainstream environmental groups lobby for legislation and litigate against polluters, and green politics opposes dirty subsidies and treats unregulated growth as ecologically blind.

cut-welfare.rationale: No environmental doctrine on welfare; green politics' social-justice pillar and Brundtland's focus on essential needs of the poor imply opposition to cuts.

worker-ownership.rationale: Green politics favours local and cooperative ownership in some strands, but worker ownership is not an environmental tenet and eco-capitalists reject it.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed; greens' grassroots democracy and nonviolence pillars suggest civil-liberties scepticism.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Environmentalism is indifferent on drug policy and green parties vary.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not an environmental question; adherents split between civil-liberties and anti-discrimination positions.

strong-leader.rationale: Green politics is built on grassroots democracy and decentralization, which are at odds with leaders bypassing gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Environmentalism relies on state regulation, legislation and treaties to protect the environment, so it rejects the idea that the state is unnecessary.

limit-guns.rationale: Green parties' nonviolence pillar suggests support for gun control, but it is not an environmental issue.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nonviolence is a green pillar and Brundtland criticises military spending as a drain, though policing is not an environmental question.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism; green parties are split.

decide-locally.rationale: Green politics emphasizes local control and bioregional democracy, though Brundtland and global problems like climate call for international action too.

rehabilitation.rationale: Not an environmental issue; the nonviolence and social-justice pillars of green politics suggest a rehabilitative lean.

traditional-family.rationale: Environmentalism has no family doctrine; adherents range from evangelical to progressive.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Green parties as part of their social-justice pillar usually back it, but it is outside the environmental core.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not environmental doctrine; green parties generally support it, while evangelical environmentalists dissent.

more-religion-public.rationale: Evangelical environmentalism exists but environmentalism is overwhelmingly secular in its politics; inferred from green parties' stance.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Environmental justice, a documented strand, holds that hazardous facilities burden minority communities and that this should be redressed.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not addressed; ecofeminist strands say yes while most environmentalists take no position.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Not an environmental question; green politics is internationalist and localist at once, and conservationists value landscape heritage.

gradual-change.rationale: Environmentalists see urgent crisis demanding rapid reform and often use protest and direct action, though mainstream groups work through institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Green politics is generally internationalist and social-justice oriented, though some population-focused environmentalists favour limits.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Brundtland called for stronger international cooperation and institutions for shared environmental problems, and the Stockholm conference and Global Greens Charter reflect this.

free-trade.rationale: Many left-wing greens are sceptical of economic globalization and some propose tariffs on fossil fuels, though Brundtland does not oppose trade as such.

nation-first.rationale: Transboundary pollution and climate change are treated as requiring global cooperation, per the Brundtland report.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Nonviolence pillar opposes force, but the issue is not environmental and adherents split.

open-borders.rationale: Not an environmental position; social-justice greens lean open, population-focused ones do not.

limit-growth.rationale: Limits to Growth, steady-state economics and green 'prosperity without growth' are documented positions, while Brundtland and bright greens favour a different, less resource-intensive growth, so a measured agree.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate is described as the leading focus of present environmentalism, and the movement is characterized by calls for urgent large-scale policy action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Bright greens stress technology and social innovation, while dark greens favour abandoning it; adherents are documented as split.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Greens mostly oppose fission under the precautionary principle, Brundtland accepted it only conditionally, and some environmentalists now support it, so adherents are split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mainstream environmentalism works through lobbying, lawsuits and protest, and green politics holds nonviolence as a pillar.

experts-over-public.rationale: Environmentalists rely on scientific expertise but green politics prizes grassroots democracy, so the two pull against one another.

central-planning.rationale: Not a mainstream environmental position; eco-socialists favour planning but green liberals and eco-capitalists reject it, and grassroots greens distrust centralization.

socialized-markets.rationale: Green strands from eco-socialist to eco-capitalist differ on ownership; this specific compromise is not a core environmental claim.

land-value-tax.rationale: Greens favour a green tax shift onto pollution and resource use, and some back land-value taxes, but this is not defining.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism; inferred from the social-justice pillar of green politics.

basic-income.rationale: Many green parties support basic income and 'prosperity without growth', but it is not an environmental core tenet.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Greens suspect globalization but protect ecology rather than domestic industry; their tariff proposals target fossil fuels.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Environmentalists want state direction of investment toward renewables and sustainability, and oppose subsidies to harmful industries.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Green politics favours local and cooperative ownership and decentralization, which loosely implies dispersed ownership.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not an environmental position; even eco-socialists rarely demand it, and Brundtland assumes continued economic growth.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Environmentalism has no such doctrine and relies on state monetary and fiscal institutions.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not an environmental position; green politics prefers grassroots democracy to state-recognized corporatist bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Green politics is founded on grassroots democracy and nonviolence, which contradict single-party rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Not addressed; the grassroots democracy pillar suggests disfavour.

democracy-best.rationale: Green politics holds grassroots and deliberative democracy as a pillar, although some radical environmentalists doubt democracy handles ecological limits.

direct-votes.rationale: Greens want citizens to directly shape decisions affecting them, through deliberative and direct democracy.

workers-councils.rationale: Eco-socialists might favour them, but green politics generally prizes citizen and community assemblies rather than workers' councils specifically.

right-to-secede.rationale: Some greens advocate bioregional democracy and urban secession, but it is not a common view.

natural-rulers.rationale: Grassroots democracy and social equality in green politics exclude rule by a naturally superior few.

political-violence-never.rationale: Nonviolence is one of the four green pillars, though radical groups like Earth First! and the ELF have used sabotage.

war-builds-character.rationale: Nonviolence is a green pillar and Brundtland treats war and nuclear arsenals as grave environmental threats.

separate-church-state.rationale: Not addressed; evangelical environmentalists ground stewardship in scripture while most others are secular.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Evangelical environmentalism grounds stewardship in scripture, but environmental law is justified on ecological and ethical grounds, not scriptural ones.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Free-market environmentalism relies on property rights and tort law, but mainstream environmentalism wants public institutions; defence is unaddressed.

military-superiority.rationale: Brundtland views military build-up as a threat to security and resources, and greens are nonviolent.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Social justice and equal moral concern pillars in green politics reject ethnic nationhood; critics of deep ecology label ethnocentric views 'eco-fascism' as out of bounds.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Only eco-socialists see class conflict as central; most environmentalists locate the driver in humanity's relation to nature.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Social justice is a green pillar, but equality of outcomes is not specified and adherents differ.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Environmentalism has been criticised for overlooking Indigenous communities, and the Brundtland report supports recognizing traditional rights over resources.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Climate-justice strands argue rich countries owe the global South, but reparations for colonization specifically are not a core claim.

civilizational-union.rationale: Not an environmental position; green politics is localist and globally cooperative.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Leopold argued that land ethics based wholly on economic self-interest are inadequate and that ethics limit freedom of action.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Leopold held natural things deserve a right to continued existence regardless of economic use, and SEP identifies intrinsic value as a central question for the field; Muir held a similar view.

limit-population.rationale: Population growth was a major concern of Ehrlich's Population Bomb and Brundtland urged lower growth, but green social-justice strands criticise coercive limits.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Dark greens hold it, but mainstream environmentalism and Brundtland seek to reform industry rather than reject it, so adherents split.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Bright greens welcome technological change, while others stress precaution and dark greens distrust it.

human-enhancement.rationale: Precautionary-principle greens are wary of new technologies; not an explicit environmental topic.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Grassroots democracy emphasis suggests disfavour, though the issue is not addressed.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Not addressed; green movements engaged in protest generally favour privacy against surveillance.

restore-past-order.rationale: Environmentalism seeks to restore ecosystems, not social orders, and is generally forward-looking in its politics.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Bright greens and science-guided environmentalists favour results while green politics is value-driven by its four pillars.

direct-action.rationale: Protests, tree-sitting and sabotage are documented tactics, yet mainstream groups use lobbying, lawsuits and elections, so adherents are split.

means-match-ends.rationale: Nonviolence and grassroots democracy as green pillars imply that the means should reflect the desired society.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Only some dark-green strands propose abandoning technology; mainstream environmentalism does not.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not an environmental position; local self-reliance greens do not demand abolition.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Brundtland prioritises essential needs of the poor, but ultimate distribution by need is not an environmental tenet.

production-for-use.rationale: Greens criticise production that ignores ecological damage and favour 'uneconomic growth' critiques, loosely supporting production for need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Eco-socialists say yes, eco-capitalists and green liberals say no.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Incompatible with nonviolence and grassroots democracy as green pillars.

collective-farming.rationale: Environmentalism favours sustainable and small-scale agriculture but not mandated collectivization.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Eco-socialists agree and eco-capitalists do not; no general environmental position.

taxation-theft.rationale: Environmental policy relies on taxes, such as green tax shifts, and rejects the view that taxation is theft.

harm-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation is justified by harm to others and to ecosystems, which fits the principle, though environmentalists also accept duties to nature beyond harm.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Leopold extends the ethical community to soils, waters, plants and animals, and Stone proposed legal standing for natural objects, so rights are not only individual human ones.

conscription.rationale: Nonviolence pillar suggests opposition, though not an environmental issue.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Green politics stresses democratic participation, not exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Environmentalism treats ecology and public goods as outside market logic and wants state stewardship.

positive-liberty.rationale: Social justice pillar and Brundtland's focus on meeting essential needs imply that material means matter to freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: Environmentalists rely on science and academia and portray industry lobbies as the powerful actors.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Rejected by the social-justice and equal-concern principles of green politics.

organic-representation.rationale: Green politics favours community-based democracy but has been organised through parties, so adherents are split.

total-state.rationale: Green politics emphasizes decentralization and grassroots democracy against total state direction.

national-rebirth.rationale: Not an environmental theme, which is global and ecological rather than national.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Environmentalism treats ecological limits and nonviolence as central, opposing expansionism.

bound-labor.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar of green politics.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Ecofeminists and critics of domination say yes, while mainstream environmentalism relies on science as reliable knowledge.

universal-morality.rationale: Environmental ethicists are split on moral universalism, with SEP surveying anthropocentric, biocentric and holist views.

single-common-good.rationale: Leopold's land ethic appeals to a common biotic community, but green politics also stresses pluralism and grassroots democracy.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism; no consistent position.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism; no consistent position.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Grassroots democracy extends to workplaces in some green strands, and labor environmentalism backs worker involvement.

school-vouchers.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism; free-market and green liberal strands differ from egalitarian ones.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Greens commonly support public investment in green transition and are not austerity-minded, though not an environmental tenet.

economic-freedom.rationale: Greens distrust growth-focused capitalism, though free-market environmentalists exist, so disagreement is mild.

national-self-determination.rationale: Green politics supports local and regional self-government, though this is not an environmental claim.

force-without-un.rationale: Greens prefer international institutions and nonviolence over unilateral force.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Science-guided environmentalism coexists with reverence for nature and evangelical stewardship, and the page notes advocates balance care with science.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Social-justice and internationalist green politics lean against excluding immigrants.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Social justice pillar and basic income support among greens suggest opposition.

class-collaboration.rationale: Eco-socialists emphasise conflict, labor environmentalism and eco-capitalists cooperation.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Conservation is an environmentalist strand about preserving natural heritage, and the ethos is protective of inherited things.

dominated-front.rationale: Not addressed, though climate-justice strands align developing countries.

workers-nation.rationale: Not an environmental question; green politics is internationalist.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar of green politics, though not an environmental issue.

ban-interest.rationale: Not addressed; some steady-state economists criticise interest-driven growth but no common position.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar and environmental justice concerns.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Only eco-socialists hold it; green liberals and others see the state as a neutral regulator.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Climate change is the leading environmental focus and greens oppose dirty subsidies and favour tariffs on fossil fuels.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Green politics is social-justice oriented and pluralist; not an environmental issue.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy claim with no basis in environmental thought and contrary to green politics' social-justice pillar.

proportional-representation.rationale: Green parties have commonly been small parties benefiting from proportional systems and endorse grassroots democracy, though sources I opened do not state it directly.

national-mission.rationale: Not an environmental theme; green politics is internationalist and nonviolent.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Ecofeminists such as Plumwood link domination of nature and of women, but this is not shared by all environmentalists.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Environmentalists criticise industry capture and anti-environmentalism, but this populist claim is not a core tenet.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar and equal moral worth, though population-control advocates are criticised for coercion.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Social justice and nonviolence pillars imply accountability, though it is not environmental.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Environmentalism relies on state legislation, regulation and international treaties to protect nature.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar of green politics.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Social justice is a green pillar, though biospheric egalitarianism in deep ecology has been criticised as misanthropic.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Not addressed by environmentalism, though Indigenous-rights concerns lean agree.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not addressed; the grassroots-freedom ethos suggests disagreement.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Environmentalists criticise livestock emissions and animal-rights thinkers like Singer and Regan extend moral consideration to animals, but a cattle ban is not a common demand.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Contrary to grassroots democracy and decentralization in green politics.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Grassroots and deliberative democracy as a green pillar imply legitimacy rests on consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilism is unrelated to environmental thought, and greens are sceptical of growth-oriented trade.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Nonviolence is a green pillar, but environmental regulation coerces property owners, and absolute libertarian framing is not shared.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Leopold's ethics as limitation on struggle and cooperation among interdependent members contrasts with this view.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Plumwood analysed domination logic against nature, and green politics values social justice; republican liberty is not named.

separated-powers.rationale: Not specific to environmentalism, but green liberals and grassroots democrats support checks and balances; litigation is a tool.

vanguard-party.rationale: Grassroots democracy is a green pillar, opposing vanguard direction.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Brundtland says essential needs of the world's poor should receive overriding priority.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labor environmentalism allies with unions and protest is a standard tactic.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Brundtland held that poverty and underdevelopment are tied to inequality and institutions, though it treated population as a pressure.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice pillar, though not an environmental topic.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Deliberative democracy supporters in green politics sometimes back sortition, but it is not a standard position.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Environmentalists favour precaution and democratic participation, though climate emergency rhetoric exists.

party-controls-media.rationale: Contrary to grassroots democracy and the open advocacy environmentalism depends on.

party-commands-army.rationale: Contrary to green pillars of nonviolence and democracy.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Some green parties have limited representatives' pay, but it is not general.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Green parties emphasise grassroots, consensus decision making rather than binding discipline.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Environmentalists favour supranational action on transboundary issues, and Brundtland urges international cooperation, though some greens are Eurosceptic.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Contrary to the decentralist, democratic emphasis of green politics.

clerical-rule.rationale: Contrary to grassroots democracy; environmentalism is mostly secular in its politics.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Nonviolence argues against war but not specifically for defeatism; not addressed.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Green grassroots democracy and nonviolence do not suggest censorship, though not addressed.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Decentralized grassroots democracy suggests suspicion of concentrated tenure, though not addressed.

recall-officials.rationale: Direct democracy emphasis implies support, though recall is not specifically described.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Nonviolence favours demilitarisation but green parties are split over alliances such as NATO.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Agrarian and back-to-nature strands value rural life while urban bright greens favour dense cities, so adherents are split.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Environmentalism relies on science and academia, although it faces criticism for elitism.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Environmental justice and Indigenous-rights concerns lean toward cultural equality, though the topic is not central.

death-penalty.rationale: Nonviolence is a green pillar, which implies opposition to executions.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Population concern and green social-justice values suggest support, though not addressed directly.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Environmentalism rests on ecological science and rejects teaching creationism, though evangelical environmentalists exist.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Not addressed; the social-justice and internationalist outlook suggests disagreement.

minority-language-support.rationale: Localist and Indigenous-supportive green politics suggests support, though not central.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Radical and counter-cultural strands of environmentalism embrace non-conformist living, but it is not a mainstream tenet.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Brundtland identified debt as a burden on developing countries' environments and development, though cancellation is not its recommendation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Deliberative democracy supports it but it is not addressed directly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Environmentalists distrust growth-first policy and hold democracy as a pillar.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Brundtland argued that meeting essential needs of the poor requires international support and that rich countries should help.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Brundtland identified nuclear war as the gravest environmental danger and Greens are nonviolent and anti-nuclear.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Direct democracy emphasis suggests support, though not addressed directly.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Nonviolence implies favouring negotiated settlements, though not addressed.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Leopold argued that ownership carries obligations to the land community beyond self-interest, and environmentalism accepts limiting property use for ecological reasons.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Leopold's land ethic puts obligations to the community above self-interest, but green politics also champions individual and social rights.

population-transfer.rationale: Contrary to the social-justice and nonviolence pillars of green politics.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Green politics applies the precautionary principle, rejecting technologies unless shown not to cause significant harm.

collective-defense.rationale: Environmentalism has no doctrine on military alliances; Brundtland stresses international cooperation and peace, but green parties have divided over NATO.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Inferred from the respect for international cooperation and self-determination in Brundtland and green politics' peace pillar; not an environmental question.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Not an environmental issue and adherents hold no common view on church-state relations.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Environmentalism is silent on the role of the head of state, so adherents are indifferent.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Inferred from green politics' nonviolence and decentralization pillars, which disfavor using force against an unwilling region.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Inferred from green politics' emphasis on decentralization and local decision-making, which favors regional autonomy.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Inferred from green politics' grassroots democracy pillar; no environmentalist strand supports divine rulers.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Inferred from green politics' social-justice pillar, which favors redistribution and progressive taxation, though ecological tax shifts are the movement's own focus.

character-from-environment.rationale: Environmentalism has no doctrine on nature versus nurture; environmental justice stresses circumstances but this is not a defining belief.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Inferred from green politics' grassroots democracy and participation, which implies rulers are accountable to law.

space-expansion.rationale: Inferred from the priority on protecting Earth's ecosystems and limits-to-growth arguments; bright-green technophiles dissent.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not an environmentalist concern; no stated position on constitutional form.

leader-cult.rationale: Inferred from green politics' grassroots democracy and nonviolence pillars, which are hostile to personality cults.

equal-parenting.rationale: Environmentalism has no custody doctrine; the social-justice pillar gives no clear direction.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Green politics rests on social justice and nonviolence rather than class war; inferred.

land-redistribution.rationale: Environmental justice and the land ethic raise ownership obligations, but there is no settled movement view on redistribution.

refugee-return.rationale: Inferred from the social-justice pillar of green politics and environmental justice concern for displaced people.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Inferred from green nonviolence, decentralization and international cooperation, which cut against territorial claims.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Inferred from the civil-liberties and social-justice pillars of green politics.

women-must-cover.rationale: Inferred from the social-justice pillar and support for equality and personal freedom in green politics.

common-currency.rationale: No environmental doctrine on currency; greens divide between support for European integration and local-currency localism.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Inferred from green stress on decentralization and local community over large political unions built on kinship.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Inferred from green support for decentralization and cultural diversity.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Environmental justice stresses minorities securing rights and protection where they live; inferred.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Leopold treats the land ethic as a moral and intellectual evolution, so ideas matter independently of production; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Green decentralization and wariness of concentrated power support breaking up cartels; inferred.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not an environmental issue and green strands divide.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Environmentalists often rely on courts and constitutional protections to constrain majorities, so the claim is inferred to be resisted.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Feminism and social justice are among green politics' pillars, and many green parties use gender quotas.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Green localism favours self-reliance, but Brundtland stresses international cooperation and trade; a closed bloc is inferred to be rejected.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Brundtland and green politics link trade and sustainable development; binding environmental standards are inferred to be favoured.

moral-incentives.rationale: Leopold stresses ethical obligation, but the movement has no doctrine on replacing material incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Nonviolence is one of the four pillars of green politics.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred from green social-justice and democratic commitments.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Environmentalism has no doctrine on history teaching; its global perspective and national attachments pull in different directions.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Environmental justice critiques colonial exploitation, and green politics stresses respect for peoples; inferred.

patriotic-education.rationale: Environmentalism is indifferent on patriotic schooling; it stresses environmental education rather than national loyalty.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Environmental justice and green politics stress social justice for disadvantaged groups, so most adherents tolerate race-conscious measures; inferred.

public-money-creation.rationale: Some green parties back monetary reform and others do not; the movement has no common position.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Greens and the ecological limits argument doubt that growth-dependent capitalism can avoid ecological crisis, though bright-green strands dissent.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Environmentalism rejects imperial claims, and green politics favours non-violence and decentralization; inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Green politics favours localization, but the Brundtland report stresses trade and international cooperation, so adherents split.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Environmental justice and global solidarity stress shared burdens, not rich-world workers as a privileged class; inferred.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Green politics holds to social justice and non-discrimination, and environmentalism has no tradition of defending a right to discriminate; inferred.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Environmentalists favour legal guarantees of rights, including a right to a healthy environment, and Brundtland urges legal protections; inferred.

missingStatements.text: Natural resources should be used only at a rate that leaves future generations able to meet their own needs.
missingStatements.rationale: The Brundtland definition of sustainable development makes intergenerational resource limits the organizing principle of environmental policy.

missingStatements.text: Governments should act on environmental risks even before there is scientific certainty that harm will occur.
missingStatements.rationale: Green politics applies the precautionary principle, rejecting technologies unless shown not to cause significant harm.

notes: Many answers are low-confidence inferences because environmentalism has little doctrine outside ecology; strands (dark green, bright green, eco-socialist, free-market) answer differently on growth, technology, nuclear and ownership.
